THOUGHT: The patient is an elderly woman who developed pruritic annular, non-scaly erythematous plaques on the extremities beginning ~2 months after starting combination immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy (pembrolizumab + ipilimumab). A short trial of oral terbinafine did not help and PAS stain was negative, making tinea corporis unlikely. The key histopathologic finding is a superficial and deep perivascular and interstitial inflammatory infiltrate with numerous eosinophils. That pattern strongly favors an eosinophil-rich drug/immune-related dermatitis rather than classic annular entities that show lymphocytic palisading (granuloma annulare) or coat‑sleeve perivascular lymphocytes (erythema annulare centrifugum). Checkpoint inhibitors are well known to cause a spectrum of cutaneous immune-related adverse events including morbilliform and eczematous eruptions and less commonly eosinophilic dermatoses (eosinophilic annular erythema–type presentations or other drug hypersensitivity reactions). Wells syndrome (eosinophilic cellulitis) can present with annular plaques and prominent eosinophils histologically, but usually has more edematous/indurated lesions and characteristic “flame figures” on biopsy (not described here). Urticarial drug eruption could show eosinophils histologically but clinically lesions are usually transient wheals rather than persistent annular plaques. Given the temporal relationship to immunotherapy, morphology, and eosinophil‑predominant infiltrate, an immune checkpoint inhibitor–related eosinophilic annular dermatitis (drug‑induced eosinophilic annular erythema) is the most likely diagnosis.

DIAGNOSIS:
1) Immune checkpoint inhibitor–related eosinophilic annular dermatitis / drug‑induced eosinophilic annular erythema (most likely)
2) Eosinophilic annular erythema (idiopathic or paraneoplastic form)
3) Drug hypersensitivity eruption (morbilliform/urticarial pattern) from pembrolizumab/ipilimumab presenting with annular configuration
4) Wells syndrome (eosinophilic cellulitis) with annular clinical appearance
5) Erythema annulare centrifugum / other annular figurate erythema (less likely given eosinophil‑predominant infiltrate and absent scale)
